newsitem.title: UK: Stg bulls unsated, wary of gains beyond 2.95 DM.
newsitem.headline: Stg bulls unsated, wary of gains beyond 2.95 DM.

text.p: Sterling bulls, who have held sway for the best part of a year, are not an easy bunch to satisfy.

The pound's 26-percent surge against the mark since August 1996 has left them thirsting for more and traders are now gunning for a move above sterling's old European Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) parity of 2.95 marks -- levels not seen in six years, analysts said on Thursday.

"All the arguments which gave rise to positive sterling sentiment are still there and given that we are only a couple of pfennigs away from the ERM central parity the risks are on the upside for the time being," said Rob Hayward, economic adviser at Bank of America.
Traders who are using technical and economic fundamentals to justify this move could, however, find these same indicators pointing south soon after the pound hits these highs.

A long-term target for sterling was 2.8650 marks, a 61.8 percent retracement of the move from the pound's highs near 3.29 in early 1989 to the record lows below 2.17 marks it set in 1995, said Steve Merrigan, chief market strategist at First Chicago in London.
The break above this level seen on Monday has cheered the bulls. The pound now needs to close the week above it to confirm their optimism.

Sterling has benefited from mounting evidence of strong British growth which has bolstered hopes of higher interest rates. Traders expect such hopes to persist in the coming weeks, and to propel sterling above the 59-month high of 2.8825 marks it set on Thursday.
At 1240 GMT it was at 2.8776/86 marks, up nearly a pfennig from the prior European close.

Merrigan predicted 2.95 marks, sterling's old ERM parity which hasn't been traded at since August 1991, would prove a psychological hurdle for sterling gains. He expects this obstacle to prove less difficult to overcome than some expect, though.
"There will be a bit of noise because it is a psychological level but it is not a classical retracement level," Merrigan said, citing 3.0125 marks as his preferred resistance.
This is a 75 percent retracement of the move from 1989 highs to the 1995 lows. It also capped sterling's attempted rebound in 1991.
Fundamental reasons to keep pushing the pound up are likely to have run out by the time sterling reaches these highs, analysts said.

Signs the British government's July 2 budget will use fiscal tightening to curb surging domestic demand -- rather than letting monetary policy do all the work -- may prove the first economic stumbling block.

"We have hit our target of 2.85 marks and while I suspect sterling could test 2.95, it will probably hit profit taking before it gets to the key level of three marks," said Steven Hannah, director of economic research at IBJ.
"If the budget is on the tight side, it will eventually weaken sterling as it will suggest rates will peak at a lower level than people are looking for."
The pound will also be vulnerable to setbacks if the loss of competitiveness that British exporters are suffering as a result of its strength starts to show up as a widening in the trade deficits.
Merrigan at First Chicago said the technical risks would also be increasingly weighted towards the downside in the months ahead.

"It looks like we'll spend a couple of months pushing higher, but then there will be a savage pullback," he said. A move below 2.76 will be the first signal of a reversal in sterling's primary uptrend, and presage a move back down to 2.60 and below, he said.
